title: Upsolve, Inc. v. James — Petition for Certiorari (No. 25-948): Is a UPL Ban Triggered by Speech About Law Content-Neutral? (Cert Denied March 30, 2026)
pub: Upsolve, Inc. v. James, petition for cert. filed, No. 25-948 (U.S. Feb. 6, 2026), cert. denied (Mar. 30, 2026)
author: Upsolve Inc. · Rev. John Udo-Okon (petitioners)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source addresses whether New York’s UPL restriction on spoken legal advice violates the First Amendment. It does not evaluate legal AI’s jagged capabilities, selective deployment, verification, human–AI work allocation or operating-model redesign, so its position on the cluster’s proposition cannot be determined.
qs: As the Second Circuit acknowledged below, Peti- tioners seek only an injunction that will allow them to talk about the law—not to draft papers or represent clients or appear in court.
That narrow focus also means that the Court can avoid any thorny questions about how the First Amendment intersects with the practice of law in gen- eral.

mo.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
Ownership reform: Investment openings may miss justice needs
Provider reform: Competition cannot overcome every access barrier

kp.k: Unmet debt-defense needs motivate nonlawyer assistance
kp.d: Petitioners describe consumer-debt litigation as an access-to-justice problem: by one cited estimate, it accounts for a quarter of lawsuits in New York’s court system, and defendants frequently fail to respond even where claims may lack merit. They argue that the state’s one-page checkbox answer form has not solved the problem and that insufficient lawyer availability motivates free, narrowly limited assistance. These are claims in an advocacy filing, not findings about AI.
qs: By one estimate, a quarter of all lawsuits in the state’s court system are attempts to collect a consumer debt.
Despite the form, though, the problem described above persists.

kp.k: Proposed volunteers provide narrowly bounded spoken legal advice
kp.d: Upsolve’s proposed American Justice Movement would train nonlawyer volunteers to help low-income defendants understand and complete New York’s consumer-debt answer form through one-on-one conversations. The proposed role excludes drafting pleadings, filing documents, and appearing in court. The source concerns human volunteers, not AI tools or automated legal service delivery.
qs: Upsolve’s volunteers would not “draft pleadings,
appear in court, or file any legal documents.”
They would just talk.

kp.k: UPL restrictions reach unpaid individualized legal conversations
kp.d: Petitioners characterize New York’s unauthorized-practice restrictions as reserving individualized legal advice to fully licensed lawyers even when advice is unpaid, exclusively spoken, and accompanied by disclaimers. They report agreement between the parties that the proposed volunteer program would violate the law. The challenge concerns New York law, not ABA Model Rules or nonlawyer ownership restrictions.
qs: New York law prohibits Upsolve’s innovative efforts to help because in New York, any one-on-one expression of legal advice—even if it is unpaid, even if it consists only of the spoken word, and no matter what disclaimers accompany it— is the practice of law and is restricted to fully licensed lawyers.
The parties here agree that Upsolve’s program, which consists solely of volunteers providing spoken advice, would be a crime.

kp.k: Both courts treated this application as regulating speech
kp.d: As reported in the petition, the district court and Second Circuit both applied Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project to recognize that the proposed activity involves speech. The Second Circuit rejected the Attorney General’s characterization of the restriction as regulating only conduct. Their disagreement concerned whether the speech restriction was content-based and therefore which level of scrutiny applied.
qs: “Plaintiffs simply wish to communicate legal advice to their potential clients regarding how to fill out New York’s one-page form for answering debt-collection actions.”
they were restrictions on speech subject to First Amendment scrutiny.

kp.k: Scrutiny standards determine preliminary protection for the program
kp.d: The district court treated the distinction between legal and nonlegal debt advice as content-based, applied strict scrutiny, and found petitioners likely to succeed. The Second Circuit instead relied on Brokamp v. James to require intermediate scrutiny, vacating the preliminary injunction and remanding for its application. The petition thus challenges a threshold standard, rather than reporting a final merits determination that the program must be permitted or prohibited.
qs: And under strict scrutiny, Petitioners were likely to succeed on the merits, which entitled them to a preliminary injunction.
The panel therefore vacated the preliminary injunction and remanded to the dis- trict court to apply intermediate scrutiny in the first instance.

kp.k: Petitioners challenge purpose-based descriptions of content restrictions
kp.d: Petitioners argue that calling a restriction one on speech’s purpose, focus, and circumstance cannot make it content-neutral when its application depends on communicating legal advice. They contend that the Second Circuit improperly equated viewpoint neutrality within legal advice with neutrality concerning subject matter. This is petitioners’ criticism of the appellate reasoning, not an independent finding.
qs: no one can have a conversation for the purpose of rendering legal opin- ions unless that conversation renders legal opinions.
“a speech regulation targeted at specific subject matter is content based even if it does not discriminate among viewpoints within that subject matter.”

kp.k: Petition alleges conflicting circuit approaches to speech restrictions
kp.d: Petitioners contrast the Second Circuit with the Third Circuit’s Schrader decision concerning child-abuse database information and the Sixth Circuit’s Catholic Charities decision concerning talk therapy. They argue those courts recognize that function or purpose can serve as a proxy for prohibited content, triggering strict scrutiny. Their asserted circuit split draws on different regulatory contexts, not multiple rulings on the same volunteer legal-advice program.
qs: But in other jurisdictions, viewpoint-neutral “function or purpose” distinctions still trigger strict scrutiny.
In the Third Circuit, that would trigger strict scrutiny; in the Second, it doesn’t.

kp.k: Licensing should not diminish ordinary speech protections
kp.d: Relying on NIFLA v. Becerra, petitioners argue that occupational licensing does not justify reduced First Amendment protection. They portray divergent lower-court treatment of counseling and other licensed activities as persistent confusion over the boundary between speech and conduct. The broader regulatory mechanism identified is licensing’s power to determine who may communicate about particular subjects.
qs: “reduce a group’s First Amendment rights by simply imposing a licensing requirement”
It is confusion about whether licensing laws require special First Amendment rules.

kp.k: Chiles could clarify licensing and speech doctrine
kp.d: At filing on February 6, 2026, petitioners predicted that the forthcoming Chiles v. Salazar decision might undermine the Second Circuit’s rationale. They requested a hold followed, if warranted, by granting, vacating, and remanding, or otherwise plenary review. This was a conditional litigation prediction; the supplied document’s heading separately records denial of certiorari on March 30, 2026.
qs: To the extent Chiles ad- dresses the intersection of licensing laws and the First Amendment, it may shed useful light on the rule articulated below.
If this Court determines a GVR is not war- ranted after Chiles, it should grant the petition for plenary review.

kp.k: Requested ruling would leave broader practice questions unresolved
kp.d: Petitioners deliberately frame the requested decision narrowly: classify a prohibition on speaking about a particular topic as content-based without resolving all First Amendment questions concerning legal practice. They emphasize that their requested injunction covers conversations rather than document drafting or courtroom representation. The petition does not propose general deregulation of legal services or establish rights for AI legal-advice systems.
qs: Peti- tioners seek only an injunction that will allow them to talk about the law—not to draft papers or represent clients or appear in court.

The only thing the Court needs to say to resolve this case is that a prohibition on speak- ing about a particular topic is a content-based re- striction on speech, leaving any other, potentially thornier questions for another day.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The petition makes no claims about AI. Its relevant legal-services claim is that trained nonlawyer volunteers could help address unmet need for assistance with consumer-debt answers, but New York’s unauthorized-practice restrictions prohibit the proposed spoken advice.
pts.d: Petitioners Upsolve and Reverend John Udo-Okon, through their counsel, describe a proposed program offering free, narrowly limited assistance to low-income defendants completing New York’s answer form. They argue that available lawyers cannot meet the need and that the form alone has not solved the problem of defendants failing to respond. Their constitutional argument is that restricting speech because it communicates legal advice is content-based. These are claims about human-delivered assistance and licensing restrictions, not AI-enabled services.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The petition relies on the underlying litigation record, an estimate of consumer-debt litigation volume, and judicial authorities; it provides no measured outcomes for the proposed volunteer program.
pts.d: Petitioners cite the appendix for the estimate that consumer-debt collection accounts for one-quarter of state lawsuits, for difficulties responding to those suits, and for the proposed program’s design. They report that the district court granted a preliminary injunction after finding likely success under strict scrutiny, while the Second Circuit vacated it and required intermediate scrutiny. These procedural rulings support the account of the regulatory dispute, not a demonstrated finding that the program improves debt-case outcomes. Petitioners also invoke First Amendment precedents to support their proposed legal standard.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The service proposal is prospective as of the February 6, 2026 petition and is limited to spoken assistance with a particular New York form.
pts.d: Petitioners seek permission for volunteers to explain the answer form and help defendants identify defenses, not to draft documents, file papers, or represent clients in court. The petition predicts that the forthcoming Chiles decision might clarify the governing First Amendment standard and support reconsideration, but expressly conditions that prediction on the grounds of that decision. The supplied document’s heading subsequently reports that certiorari was denied on March 30, 2026; that is not a merits determination endorsing or rejecting the petitioners’ claims.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate affected groups are low-income New Yorkers facing consumer-debt lawsuits, Upsolve, and prospective nonlawyer volunteers.
pts.d: Petitioners describe defendants at risk of default judgments who need assistance understanding and completing the state-provided answer form. Upsolve would organize and train volunteers; Reverend Udo-Okon wishes to help his congregants with legal problems. Petitioners argue that New York’s licensing restrictions prevent these volunteers from offering individualized spoken legal advice even without payment. The asserted benefit is improved access to civil legal assistance, rather than enterprise cost savings or changes to law-firm staffing.
